meaning: The Large-Jawed One — the monkey-god of devotion and strength, Rāma's peerless servant

phonemes.desc: Voiced glottal breath [ɦ] — softer than English 'h' — with short open [ɐ]
Short [n] and [ʊ]; the middle syllable is quick and light, almost swallowed
Voiced bilabial [m] plus long open [aː]; the macron marks length and gives the name its Tier-1 weight

pronunciation.approximation: 'huh-noo-MAHN' — the final syllable long, the 'h' a soft breath rather than an English hiss.

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: हनुमान् (hanumān), possessive of hanu-, 'jaw, cheek' (Monier-Williams s.v.) — 'the large-jawed one'; his birth-name Añjaneya recalls his mother Añjanā

kin.label: Indo-European
kin.form: Cognate with Greek γένυς (génys), 'jaw' — both from PIE *ǵenh₂us; compare Latin gena 'cheek' and English 'chin'

kin.label: Regional forms
kin.form: Māruti/Maruti ('son of the wind'), Tamil Añjanēyar, Thai Hanuman (หนุมาน)

pronunciation.note: Hanumān is Tier 1 because the long final ā is preserved — the one feature ASCII 'Hanuman' loses. The name is the possessive of hanu 'jaw', the mark left when Indra's thunderbolt broke the child's jaw.

domains.title: The Son of the Wind
domains.subtitle: Devotion, Strength, the Leap, and the Burning of Laṅkā
domains.lead: Hanumān is the god of what devotion makes possible: strength that serves, courage that leaps oceans, and humility that calls itself only a messenger. The wind-god's son, Rāma's servant, and the Rāmāyaṇa's engine — whenever the quest stands at the water's edge, he is the one who jumps.

cards.name: The Leap
cards.desc: One bound from India to Laṅkā — devotion as the only wings needed.

cards.name: The Mountain
cards.desc: The herb-mountain he carried through the night sky to save Lakṣmaṇa.

cards.name: The Burning Tail
cards.desc: Set alight by Rāvaṇa — and used to torch golden Laṅkā itself.

cards.name: The Gada
cards.desc: His mace: strength in service, never for its own sake.

symbols.name: The mace (gada)
symbols.meaning: Strength subordinated to service; he carries it as Rāma's general, never as a warlord of his own

symbols.name: The flying mountain-bearer
symbols.meaning: The night flight with the healing mountain in one hand — the most reproduced scene in Indian devotional art

symbols.name: The torn-open chest
symbols.meaning: In later devotional tradition (the Ānand Rāmāyaṇa and its heirs), he splits his own breast to show Rāma and Sītā enthroned where his heart was

symbols.name: The sindoor-covered body
symbols.meaning: Devotees smear him with vermilion as Sītā once did; he wore it as armor, and his idols wear it still

symbols.name: The upraised tail
symbols.meaning: His tail — bound in oil-soaked rags and set alight by Rāvaṇa's court, then used to burn Laṅkā itself

mythology.lead: Hanumān's mythology is drawn almost entirely from the Rāmāyaṇa, where he enters late and transforms everything: a minor forest-dweller who becomes the epic's decisive force. His stories are the anatomy of bhakti — what devotion can carry, leap, burn, and endure — and the reason the tradition made him the most beloved god of the North Indian street.

myths.title: The Wind's Son
myths.text: Hanumān's origin story is told by the old bear Jāmbavān, on the seashore before the great leap, when the vanaras doubted that anyone could cross the ocean (Rāmāyaṇa, Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa 65–67, vulgate). As an infant, the child of the wind-god Vāyu and the vanara woman Añjanā saw the rising sun, mistook it for a ripe fruit, and leapt to eat it. Indra hurled his thunderbolt; it broke the child's jaw — hanu, the bone that named him — and the wounded wind, in grief, withdrew his breath from the worlds until the gods repaired the harm with boons: from Indra, the bolt could not kill him; from Agni, fire could not burn; from Varuṇa, water could not drown; from Brahmā, immunity from every weapon. And a curse laid on him in childhood erased his own memory of that strength until someone should remind him — a forgetting the epic needs, so that Jāmbavān can do the reminding. The myth builds his whole character in one scene: the audacity to leap at the sun, and the gift that such leaps are always available once they are named.

myths.title: One Bound to Laṅkā
myths.text: When Sītā was carried across the ocean, the vanara army reached the shore and stopped: a hundred yojanas of water and no way across. The elder Jāmbavān reminded Hanumān of his strength; Hanumān grew until he filled the sky, pressed down on the mountain Mahendra with his foot, and leapt — clearing the ocean in a single bound (Rāmāyaṇa, Sundarakāṇḍa 1). He landed on Laṅkā's Trikūṭa hill, shrank himself to the size of a cat, and searched the golden city street by street, palace by palace, until he found Sītā beneath an Aśoka tree, guarded but unbowed. He dropped Rāma's ring before her like a signature, heard her story, fought his way out, and returned with the report that turned a rescue into a war. The crossing is the epic's hinge: geography made absolute is dissolved by a single act of faith. And the ocean itself, in the later tellings, asked the mountain for the recoil of that leap — even the elements wanted a share in the story.

myths.title: The Tail that Burned a City
myths.text: In Laṅkā, Hanumān let himself be taken — to measure the enemy, he said — and was dragged in his bonds before Rāvaṇa. Their exchange is one of the epic's great set-pieces: the captured monkey lecturing the ten-headed king on statecraft, diplomacy, and the certainty of his own destruction (Rāmāyaṇa, Sundarakāṇḍa 20–21). Rāvaṇa's courtiers had his tail wrapped in oil-soaked cloth and set it alight. Hanumān grew; the bonds snapped; and with his own burning tail for a torch he leapt from mansion to mansion until golden Laṅkā — Rāvaṇa's pride and Sītā's prison — was a sheet of flame (Sundarakāṇḍa 52–54). Only the Aśoka grove and the captive herself were spared, by the grace of the fire-goddess; then he plunged his scorched tail into the sea. The lesson the epics repeat most often is here in its purest form: what your enemy kindles for your shame, carry as your weapon. The fire meant to display him became the instrument that announced the war.

myths.title: The Night Flight
myths.text: Lakṣmaṇa lay dying, struck by Indrajit's spear, and the physician Suṣeṇa named the cure: the saṃjīvana herb, growing on a Himalayan peak, to be brought before sunrise. Hanumān flew north through the night — and on the mountain, unable to identify one herb among ten thousand in the dark, he did the thing only he could do: he wrapped his arms around the mountain's root, broke it free, and lifted the whole peak into the sky (Rāmāyaṇa, Yuddhakāṇḍa 74–76). The herbs on the carried mountain healed Lakṣmaṇa, and the flying figure with a peak in one hand became the most painted scene in Indian religious art, sold in his temple shops to this day. He did not hesitate at the impossible identification; he widened the solution until it included the whole problem. The image endures because it is exact theology: devotion does not need to know which herb — it needs only to bring the entire mountain.

myths.title: The Immortal Servant
myths.text: At the war's end, when Rāma had taken his throne and the rewards were given, Hanumān refused every gift. His lord's presence was his wage, he said; to serve Rāma was its own fruit. Rāma answered with a boon that solved the refusal: Hanumān would live as long as the story of Rāma was told — present at every recitation, at every reading, wherever and whenever a single person spoke the epic (Rāmāyaṇa, Yuddhakāṇḍa; the boon is elaborated in the later Rāmcaritmānas tradition). It is the most enviable immortality in Hindu mythology, and deliberately so: not endless life, but endless employment in the work he loves. The Tulsīdās tradition made the promise a fact of daily life — every recitation of the Hanumān Chālīsā is one more payment on the boon — and his images still stand at the back of Rāma temples, where a servant may hear the story forever. The epic's last word on devotion is that it outlives its reward: Rāma returned to heaven, and Hanumān stayed to listen.

lore.syncretism: He crosses every boundary: in Cambodia's Reamker and Thailand's Ramakien he is the monkey-general unchanged; China's classical tradition links him to the monkey-king Sūn Wùkōng of Journey to the West (the kinship debated for a century); and Indonesia keeps Hanoman as the Ramayana's most-beloved wayang character. The wrestler-god is also the celibate scholar — patron of gyms (akhāṛās) and grammar students alike. In the Khmer, Thai, Lao, and Balinese retellings, he is so beloved that the epics are, in places, his story: the Reamker spends whole books inside his adventures. No other Hindu god is so completely at home in the languages of five nations.
lore.culturalLegacy: The Hanumān Chālīsā — Tulsīdās's forty verses — is the most-recited hymn in the Hindi world; his Tuesday fasts, his sindoor-red idols, and his roar in a hundred TV serials make him the most-worshipped deity of North India. 'Bajrang Bali' is the name shouted at heavy lifts and hard exams alike. The Indian Army's mountain troops invoke him; his flying figure brands logistics firms, gyms, and the Delhi Metro's most-photographed statue (108 ft at Karol Bagh). Wrestlers anoint him before matches; students before examinations; the frightened at crossroads at dusk. Of all the gods of the Rāmāyaṇa, it is the servant — not the king — whom the streets claim as their own.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Hanumān is the god of the impossible errand. He never asks whether the ocean can be crossed — he asks for Rāma's name and jumps. He is the proof the Rāmāyaṇa makes everywhere it goes: that the measure of strength is not what it can lift but whom it serves, and that the biggest tasks are always done by the ones who say 'I am only the messenger.'

The wrestlers know him as the patron of strength; the students as the patron of grammar; the frightened as the name that ends fear. He is all three, because his real gift is neither muscle nor memory but this: the certainty that the ocean can be crossed, spoken in the ear of anyone who is sure it cannot.

The Jāmbavān moment is the one India loves most: before the leap, the old bear reminds him of his strength — because the curse had made him forget. Everyone keeps a Hanumān inside, a strength mislaid until someone says its name aloud. The whole Chālīsā is, in a way, that reminder set to verse.

lore.archaeology: His oldest images are Gupta-period (5th c. CE) reliefs; the cult's medieval explosion runs through the Vijayanagara empire, whose emblem he was. The great modern colossi — Karol Bagh (Delhi, 108 ft), Nandura (105 ft), Paritala Anjaneya (135 ft, among the world's tallest statues) — continue the tradition of the Vijayanagara monoliths. The Sankat Mochan temple at Vārāṇasī (16th c., founded within Tulsīdās's tradition) and Hampi's Anjaneya hill anchor his pilgrimage map.
